specPoints.text: know reactions, including ionic equations where appropriate, for identifying: i carbonate ions, CO 3 2- , and hydrogencarbonate ions, HCO - 3 , using an aqueous acid to form carbon dioxide (and testing the gas with limewater) ii sulfate ions, SO 2- 4 , using acidified barium chloride solution iii ammonium ions, NH + 4 , using sodium hydroxide solution and warming to form ammonia (and testing with litmus and HCl fumes)

primer.text: Three ion tests cover most of qualitative inorganic analysis: ammonia released from ammonium ions, fizzing carbon dioxide from carbonates, and the white barium sulfate clue to sulfate ions. This note gives the overall and ionic equations for each test plus the observation that seals the identification.

lessons.title: The three-ion toolkit
lessons.opening: Three simple test-tube reactions identify most of qualitative analysis: ammonium, carbonate (plus hydrogencarbonate) and sulfate. This lesson sets the toolkit's ground rules - dissolve solids in deionised water first, then run the identity reactions with their ionic equations.
keyPoints: Test tube reactions identify ammonium, carbonate, hydrogencarbonate and sulfate ions.
Solid samples must first dissolve in deionised water to make an aqueous solution.
Each test pairs an overall equation with its ionic equation showing the reacting ions.
The ammonium test releases ammonia gas; the carbonate test releases carbon dioxide.
The sulfate test precipitates white barium sulfate from acidified solution.

low.restatement: Dissolve, then test: ammonia for ammonium, fizzing limewater for carbonate, white barium sulfate for sulfate - three ions, three signatures.
low.analogy: Three doorbells on one corridor: each button (reagent) rings exactly one bell (ion), and the sound (observation) names the room.
low.examPointer: Write ionic equations without spectators - the spectator-free form is what the question means by 'ionic equation'.

medium.restatement: Each ionic equation isolates the reacting pair: NH4+ with OH-, H+ with CO3 2- or HCO3-, and Ba2+ with SO4 2-; everything else in the tube is a spectator whose removal defines the ionic form.
medium.analogy: A duet extracted from an orchestra: the ionic equation prints only the two soloists (reacting ions) and silences the orchestra (spectators).
medium.examPointer: When asked for both equations, give the full molecular one and the ionic one separately - merging them loses structure marks.

check.stem: Which ions can simple test tube reactions identify?

options.explanation: The three-test toolkit covers all four.
Halide testing needs silver nitrate, not this toolkit.
The toolkit is three tests, not universal.

check.stem: What must happen to a solid sample before testing?

options.text: It must dissolve in deionised water to make an aqueous solution
It must be heated to melting
It must be acidified with concentrated acid first
options.explanation: Only the sulfate test acidifies, and dilute at that.

check.stem: What does an ionic equation omit?

options.text: The spectator ions that take no part in the reaction

options.explanation: Water stays when it is a product.
Charges are essential to the ionic form.

check.stem: Which gas does the carbonate test release?

options.explanation: That is the ammonium test's gas.
No oxygen forms in this test.

check.stem: Which reagent identifies sulfate ions?

options.explanation: That is the ammonium test's reagent.

check.stem: State the three ion tests in the toolkit.
check.modelAnswer: Ammonium ions with sodium hydroxide and warming, carbonate ions with aqueous acid, and sulfate ions with acidified barium chloride.

check.stem: Write the ionic equation for carbonate meeting acid.
Explain why deionised water is specified for dissolving samples.
check.modelAnswer: Tap water carries its own ions, including carbonate and sulfate, which would trigger false positives; deionised water adds no interfering ions.

check.stem: A solution gives no ammonia, no fizz, but a white precipitate with acidified barium chloride. Which ion is present, and which two are absent?
check.modelAnswer: Sulfate is present; ammonium and carbonate are absent by their negative tests.

lessons.title: Ammonium and carbonate, observed
lessons.opening: Two gas-producing tests side by side. This lesson runs ammonium with warm sodium hydroxide to damp red litmus turning blue, and carbonate with dilute acid to limewater turning milky - overall equations, ionic equations, observations.
keyPoints: Ammonium ions plus sodium hydroxide release ammonia on warming, turning damp red litmus blue.
The ammonium ionic equation is NH4+ + OH- -> NH3 + H2O.
Ammonia also forms white smoke of ammonium chloride with concentrated HCl fumes.
Carbonate ions plus acid release CO2, which turns limewater milky.
The carbonate ionic equation is 2H+ + CO3 2- -> CO2 + H2O, with the hydrogencarbonate variant H+ + HCO3-.

low.restatement: Warm ammonium with alkali and the fumes turn red litmus blue; add acid to a carbonate and pipe the fizz into limewater until it goes milky.
low.analogy: Two kettles: one whistles ammonia (blue litmus), the other puffs CO2 (milky limewater) - each kettle rings only its own gas.
low.examPointer: State the warming explicitly in the ammonium test - the reaction needs the water bath to release enough ammonia.

medium.restatement: Both tests are gas-mobilisation reactions: OH- deprotonates NH4+ to volatile NH3, and H+ protonates CO3 2- (or HCO3-) to volatile CO2; the follow-up confirmations - litmus and limewater - fingerprint each gas independently.
medium.analogy: Two escape ramps off the same highway: alkali frees the ammonia cargo, acid frees the carbon dioxide cargo, and the checkpoint tests (litmus, limewater) log which cargo escaped.
medium.examPointer: Give the hydrogencarbonate variant H+ + HCO3- -> CO2 + H2O when the question names HCO3- explicitly.

check.stem: What observation confirms ammonium ions?

options.text: Damp red litmus paper turning blue near the warmed tube
options.explanation: Ammonia's alkaline fumes flip the litmus.

check.stem: Which reagent releases ammonia from ammonium salts?

options.explanation: Limewater is a CO2 detector, not a releaser.

check.stem: What white smoke forms when ammonia meets concentrated HCl fumes?

options.explanation: The smoke is the salt, not steam.

check.stem: What does the limewater test confirm after the carbonate fizz?

options.text: The gas is carbon dioxide, from the milky precipitate
options.explanation: CO2 + limewater gives the white suspension.
Hydrogen does not react with limewater.
The milkiness is the positive result.

check.stem: Which ionic equation covers the hydrogencarbonate test?

options.explanation: One proton suffices for the hydrogencarbonate.

check.stem: Write the ammonium ionic equation.
State the carbonate test's full molecular equation with sodium carbonate.
Explain why warming is essential in the ammonium test.
check.modelAnswer: The deprotonation equilibrium releases little ammonia cold; the water bath heats the mixture, driving enough NH3 out of solution to reach the litmus and flip it blue.

check.stem: How many protons does one CO3 2- ion absorb to become one CO2 plus one water, and what charge balance does the ionic equation show?
check.modelAnswer: Two protons balance the 2- ion: 2H+ + CO3 2- closes charge at zero on both sides.

lessons.title: The sulfate test and the acid-first rule
lessons.opening: One precipitate, one guard rail. This lesson runs acidified barium chloride onto the sample, reads the white BaSO4 as the positive sign, and explains why the hydrochloric acid must go in first.
keyPoints: Acidify the sample with dilute hydrochloric acid before adding barium chloride.
A white precipitate of barium sulfate confirms sulfate ions: Ba2+ + SO4 2- -> BaSO4.
The acid-first rule removes carbonates that would otherwise precipitate barium carbonate and confuse the result.
Barium chloride supplies the Ba2+ that pairs with SO4 2-.
The white precipitate is the test's only positive reading.

low.restatement: Acid first, then barium: any carbonate fizz clears the stage, and only true sulfate stays to meet the barium and drop as white BaSO4.
low.analogy: Sweeping the stage before the audition: the acid removes the carbonate understudies so only the sulfate lands the white-costume role.
low.examPointer: Name the interference and its removal in one sentence - carbonates would also precipitate with Ba2+, so acid removes them first.

medium.restatement: Acidification protonates any CO3 2- to volatile CO2 before barium arrives, so the only anion left able to precipitate Ba2+ is SO4 2-; hydrochloric acid is specified because its own barium salt stays soluble.
medium.analogy: Clearing the guest list before the VIP arrives: the acid escorts the carbonate out the door, and barium only ever meets sulfate in the room.
medium.examPointer: Answer 'why HCl and not H2SO4' if asked: sulfuric acid would add sulfate ions of its own and force a false positive.

check.stem: What is the positive observation of the sulfate test?

options.text: A white precipitate of barium sulfate

check.stem: Which reagent pair runs the sulfate test?

options.text: Dilute hydrochloric acid first, then aqueous barium chloride

options.explanation: The acid would add sulfate ions.

check.stem: Why must the acid be added before the barium chloride?

options.text: To remove carbonates that would otherwise precipitate and interfere
options.explanation: Clearing the interferent first keeps the reading honest.
Speed is not the point; accuracy is.

check.stem: Which ionic equation describes the positive test?

options.explanation: The two ions pair into the white solid.
That is the interference reaction, not the test.
Barium chloride is soluble, so no precipitate forms.

check.stem: Why is hydrochloric acid specified rather than sulfuric acid?

options.text: Sulfuric acid would introduce sulfate ions and force a false positive
options.explanation: The chosen acid must carry no sulfate.
The barium chloride does the precipitating.

check.stem: Write the sulfate test's ionic equation.
check.modelAnswer: Ba2+ (aq) + SO4 2- (aq) -> BaSO4 (s), the white precipitate.

check.stem: State what the acid-first step removes and how.
check.modelAnswer: It removes carbonate ions, converting them to carbon dioxide gas before the barium chloride is added.

check.stem: Explain why barium carbonate would mimic the sulfate result.
check.modelAnswer: Ba2+ precipitates with CO3 2- as white barium carbonate, an observation indistinguishable from barium sulfate; removing carbonate first eliminates the mimic.

check.stem: A sample fizzes with acid and later gives a white precipitate with barium chloride even though acid was added first and the fizz stopped. Which ion caused the fizz and which caused the precipitate?
check.modelAnswer: The fizz came from carbonate (cleared as CO2); the later white precipitate confirms sulfate was present all along.

glossary.definition: The reaction written with only the participating ions, spectators omitted.
Calcium hydroxide solution that turns milky with carbon dioxide, confirming carbonate ions upstream.
The sulfate-test protocol of acidifying before adding barium chloride so carbonates cannot mimic the white precipitate.
